alternatives: Make Chung's inventory the Chamorro inventory (a, ɒ; ɾ; no ɡʷ), respelling the rows of Blust (2000).

question: Dougherty (2024: 111-121) gives the Yapese vowels with IPA that differs from Jensen's (1977a) symbols entered here: ë/ea /æ(ː)/ (here ɛ), o/oo /o(ː)/ (here ɔ), ä/ae (here æ), ö/oe /ɵ(ː)/, a/aa /ɑ(ː)/. Which do his rows use?
chosen_reading: Match by the Yapese spelling, which both give: ë/ea = ɛ, o/oo = ɔ, ä/ae = æ, as in the Yapese inventory (decision jensen1977-vowels); Dougherty's IPA is kept in source_form.
alternatives: Change the Yapese vowel symbols to Dougherty's (ë = æ, o = o), respelling Jensen's inventory.

question: Mayer (2025: 55-70) gives Woleaian 17 consonants, 9 marginal geminates and 8 vowels, with other symbols and values than the inventory of Tawerilmang & Sohn (1984) used here: b a voiced stop /b/ (here ɸ), apical post-alveolar ʃ̺ t͡ʃ̺ ɾ̺ (here ʂ ʈ͡ʂ r), the tap ɾ (here l), ʉ (here ɨ), and short and long œ, ɒ (here long-only əː, ɔː); no pʷ (Tawerilmang & Sohn's pw, here a phoneme, is one of his allophones of /b/). Which inventory should Woleaian show?
chosen_reading: Keep the inventory of Tawerilmang & Sohn (1984), with Mayer's allophones entered on the phonemes the two share and his analysis noted on the lect (sheet edit), until the user decides.
alternatives: Make Mayer's inventory the Woleaian inventory, with his marginal geminates, and respell the Woleaian rows of Bender et al. (2003a) and the allophones to it.

question: Mayer (2025: 72-74, Table 2.16) proposes Proto-Chuukic vowels *i *ʉ *u *e *o *æ *a *ɔ, with *e > ə, ɞ (e) in Central Chuukic, and gives cognates for them (Table 2.17). Enter them?
chosen_reading: Not entered: Proto-Chuukic here has the vowels it inherits from PMc, and Mayer marks the proposal as tentative ('a full-fledged analysis ... is beyond the scope of this grammar', p. 72).
alternatives: Enter the proposal as a second vowel system of Proto-Chuukic (system Mayer), with the vowel rows of Woleaian and the other Chuukic lects of Table 2.17 against it.

question: Which symbols for Roddy's (2007) Satawalese labialized-velarized consonants and affricate, and do the rows of Bender et al. (2003a) follow them?
chosen_reading: pʷˠ, mʷˠ = pʷ, mʷ (as in the other Chuukic lects); the affricate t͡ʃ as printed. After landing, the Satawalese rows of Bender et al. (2003a) are respelled: ʈ͡ʂ > t͡ʃ, x > ɡ (Roddy's g, with [x] its allophone), l > n (Roddy's [l] is a free variant of n), with the old symbol in source_form (sheet edits).
alternatives: pʷˠ, mʷˠ as printed; keep the rows' symbols and accept the warnings.

question: Which IPA for van den Berg's (2014) Hatohobeian and Sonsorolese bw, mw, pw, ü, gl and r?
chosen_reading: bw, mw, pw = bʷ, mʷ, pʷ (her velarized [bˠ mˠ pˠ], written ʷ as in the other Chuukic lects, which describe the same sounds as labialized and velarized); ü = ɨ; gl = ɡˡ (lateral velar); r = ɾ (her tap); ts = t͡ʃ. After landing, the Sonsorolese rows of Bender et al. (2003a) are respelled where they write the same sounds differently: l > ɡˡ (and the allophone row of Oda 1977 on l moves to ɡˡ), r > ɾ, d > ð (sheet edits).
alternatives: bˠ, mˠ, pˠ as printed; gl = ɫ; keep Bender's l and r in the rows.

question: Which symbols for Ellis's (2012) Saipan Carolinian bʷˠ, mʷˠ, pʷˠː and ʈʂ͡:ʲ, and are the Carolinian rows of Bender et al. (2003a) respelled to them?
chosen_reading: bʷˠ, mʷˠ, pʷˠː = bʷ, mʷ, pʷː (as in the other Chuukic lects); ʈʂ͡:ʲ = ʈ͡ʂː, the palatalization mark dropped (it only keeps the symbol in Woleaian's column, p. 151). The rows of Bender et al. (2003a) already write these sounds as Ellis does (bʷ, ʂ, x, l), so none needs respelling; the orthography note of caro1242 changes to IPA with Ellis's inventory (sheet edit). The rows of Jackson (1984, 1986) with k, ʈ͡ʂ and pʷ (single) keep their symbols and give warnings: Ellis has these only as geminates.
alternatives: Keep Ellis's symbols as printed (bʷˠ, ʈʂ͡:ʲ); or respell the k, ʈ͡ʂ, pʷ rows of Jackson to kː, ʈ͡ʂː, pʷː.

question: How are the dialects of Jackson & Marck (1991) entered: the southern EL (Elle) and LN (Elle-Enne) dialects and Tanapag (Enne)?
chosen_reading: Carolinian (caro1242) is the southern speech of Ellis's (2012) inventory, the EL dialect; LN's n is a marginal phoneme and an allophone row of l, not a lect of its own, since the sources give no inventory or rows for it. Tanapag stays the dialect tana1281 with the rows of Bender et al. (2003a); its spelling differences (n for l, rh for sch, h for s, g for gh; Ellis 2012: 9) go into its notes (sheet edit).
alternatives: Make EL and LN dialect lects under Carolinian; or treat Tanapag as a separate language (Talaabog), as Ellis (2012: 10-11) prefers.

question: What enters from Rehg's (1993) Proto-Micronesian: long vowels, t', and the prosodic rules?
chosen_reading: Rehg's symbols as the spelling system 'Rehg' of PMc (s' = *s, s = *S, t' = *c; no *T, *Z, *y); the final short high vowel devoicing as allophones of *i, *u; stress, pitch and phrase-initial lengthening in the PMc notes. The long vowels ('the same five (short and long) vowels', p. 26) are not added as phonemes: every lect below PMc that inherits by assumption would then carry five implied long vowels.
alternatives: Add *iː *eː *aː *oː *uː to PMc (with the optional final long vowel shortening as allophones); read t' as another consonant.

question: Where does Nguluwan (Sakiyama 1982) go in the tree?
chosen_reading: A dialect of Yapese (language_id yape1248, parent POc like Yapese), as Sakiyama 'can define it' (p. 106), with its own Glottocode ngul1236.
alternatives: A language beside Yapese, as Glottolog 5.4 has it, under a new group Yapic (yape1250) holding Yapese and Nguluwan (Yapese's tree_parent would change); or a language directly under POc.

question: Which IPA for Sakiyama's (1982) Nguluwan ch, ä, b and g?
chosen_reading: ch = t͡ʃ (no value given; paired with j [dʒ] in the chart); ä = ɐ (the typed bracket letter is a turned a); b and g = b, ɡ (charted as voiced stops, not as the fricatives of Yapese b, g).
alternatives: ch = ʈ as in Yapese (Jensen 1977a); ä = ʌ; b, g = β, ɣ.

question: How do the analyses of Vita & Pedro (2021) that differ from van den Berg (2014) enter Sonsorolese?
chosen_reading: Van den Berg's inventory stays. Their ʝ (voiced palatal fricative) for her j, their view that ə is phonemic (xəɣə- 'tie up' in careful speech, p. 36), the seven diphthongs (Table 3) and the short final vowels ɨ̆ ʉ̆ ŏ ɐ̆ (Table 2) go into notes (sheet edits); their alphabet (Table 6) into the orthography note.
alternatives: Replace van den Berg's j with ʝ and drop the marginal mark on ə.

question: Is Blust's (1991: 88) Proto-Philippines (Figure 2: p t k q b d z j g m n ñ ŋ s h l r R w y; vowels i u e a) entered?
chosen_reading: No: there is no Proto-Philippines node. Philippine subgroups (Proto-Batanic, Proto-Northern Luzon, Proto-Central Luzon, PGCPh, Proto-Manide-Alabat) sit under PMP, and Blust's PPh > microgroup statements (p. 89) and Table 2 are entered against those nodes where the lect exists.
alternatives: A node Proto-Philippines (pph) under PMP with Figure 2 as its inventory, the Philippine nodes moved under it (and Sangiric, Minahasan, which Blust 1991 counts as Philippine), with alt_parents for the classifications that reject the group.

question: How are Blust's (1991) Greater Central Philippines members entered?
chosen_reading: PGCPh (grea1284, already under PMP) keeps its daughters (Umiray Dumaget, Proto-Subanen, Molbog). Central Philippines, South Mangyan, Palawanic, Manobo, Danaw and Gorontalo-Mongondow are not nodes, and the Table 2 languages that are not lects (Tagalog, Bikol, Hanunóo, Palawan Batak, Cebuano, Mansaka, Western Bukidnon Manobo, Maranao, Bolaang Mongondow, Gorontalo, and outside GCP Gaddang, Ilokano, Bontok, Pangasinan, Sambal, Kalamian Tagbanwa, Inati, Tiruray, Samal, Proto-Sangiric, Proto-Minahasan) are not added for one row each.
alternatives: Add them as lects with their *R row (they would be treated as assumed-unchanged, having fewer than 13 phonemes known); add the six microgroups as nodes.

question: Are the families of Grimes & Grimes (1987) entered as groups under Proto-South Sulawesi?
chosen_reading: No: the seven daughters of Mills (1975) sit directly under PSS. Grimes & Grimes's Northern South Sulawesi Family (Mandar, Mamuju, PUS, Pattae', the Toraja-Sa'dan and Masenrempulu Subfamilies) and Mills's 'Toraja, in the broadest sense, including PUS-Seko and Sa'dan' (1975: 217-218) each contain a group the other splits, and neither is a reconstructed node, so neither can be an alternative node (alt_parents must be a proto-language). Their other families each hold one lect of the database. Their classification is in the lect notes.
alternatives: Enter Makassar, Bugis, Northern South Sulawesi, Toraja-Sa'dan and Masenrempulu as `group` nodes (tree_parent) after Grimes & Grimes and Glottolog, with Mills's grouping in the notes.

question: How is Mills's (1975) Proto-South Sulawesi placed and its PAN > PSS changes entered?
chosen_reading: PSS under PMP, Glottocode blank (Glottolog 5.4's South Sulawesi, sout3413, has no Seko and adds Tamanic; Greater South Sulawesi adds Rampi and Badaic). Mills's PAN (Dempwolff's notation) is restated against PMP: PAN *h = PMP *q (n. 4), Dempwolff's *g of the RLD law = PMP *j (> PSS *z). Rows only for the changes Mills states (PMP *e > *ə, the final diphthongs and *-iq, *-uq, *j > *z, *R > *r and final *R); the lect's `inherit` is blank, so PMP phonemes Mills does not discuss are unentered for PSS.
alternatives: PSS under Proto-Celebic or a Greater South Sulawesi node; inherit assumed-unchanged (PMP *z and *h, which share symbols with PSS *z and *h of different origin, would then be implied wrongly).

question: Which lects carry Mills's (1975) language groups Mass., PUS and Seko, and the Makasar dialects?
chosen_reading: Mass. on Duri (duri1242), whose dialects Cakke and Kalosi supply most of the forms, as varieties; PUS on Glottolog's family pitu1237 and Seko on seko1241 (a family under Rampi-Seko-Badaic in Glottolog), each as one language, with SekoL (Lemo) and SekoP (Padang) as varieties; Konjo and Salayar as varieties of Makasar, as Mills has them. All seven directly under PSS. Mamuju (Appendix only) is not entered.
alternatives: Separate lects for Duri Cakke (cakk1237), Duri Kalosi (kalo1260), Seko Padang (seko1243) and Seko Tengah (seko1242, if Lemo is there); a Massenrempulu language node.

question: Which IPA for Mills's (1975) daughter-language letters c, j, y, ñ, ng, q, ë?
chosen_reading: c, ɟ, j, ɲ, ŋ, ʔ, ə: j as the voiced palatal stop, as Jukes (2020: 66) has it for Makasar; y the glide.
alternatives: j as d͡ʒ and c as t͡ʃ in Bugis and the northern languages.

question: Tryon (2010: 289) says the Santo languages 'appear more closely related to each other than to languages from any island outside Santo and so to constitute a Santo subgroup within Northern Vanuatu', on 'tentative shared phonological and lexical innovation'. Is a Santo group entered?
chosen_reading: No: Tryon gives no innovations, and the Santo lects of the database (Sakao, Tamambo, Araki) stay under Proto-North-Central Vanuatu. The language list goes into their notes (sheet edits).
alternatives: A `group` Santo (Espiritu Santo) under PNCV holding Sakao, Tamambo and Araki.

question: How are Adelaar's (1981) Batak reconstruction and correspondences entered beside Billings & McDonnell (2024)?
chosen_reading: Billings & McDonnell's nodes stay (pnb = Adelaar's Proto-Northern-Batak; pcsb = his Proto-Southern-Batak with Simalungun; psb = his Proto-Toba; his Proto-Angkola-Mandailing is not entered, as their AM-Batak is not). Adelaar's dialect correspondences are composed onto the node that all daughters showing them share, as a second source beside Billings & McDonnell's rows; new is *t > NB c before i, entered with Adelaar's *t > t elsewhere (§9.2). The SB loss of intervocalic *w (§8.2: To ak < **awak, Toba has no semivowels) is not entered: it would cancel Billings & McDonnell's stated retention of *w in Toba, Angkola and Mandailing. His dialect inventories go in for Dairi, Toba, Angkola, Mandailing and Simalungun (Karo keeps Woollams 2005); Toba and Angkola (h) is an allophone of /k/. Simalungun j is Adelaar's voiced palatal stop ɟ, so Billings & McDonnell's sporadic Simalungun d͡ʒ shows as a reflex outside the inventory; so do their Toba h (an allophone of /k/ for Adelaar), j and w (Toba has no semivowels, §3.1). Part III (PAN > PB) is not entered: Billings & McDonnell already state PSUM > PB, and Adelaar's PAN (Dyen's) does not map onto PMP one to one (*Z > PB *d beside *z > PB *j).
alternatives: Rename the nodes after Adelaar (Proto-Southern-Batak for pcsb, Proto-Toba for psb); add Proto-Angkola-Mandailing; enter Part III as PB rows against PSUM.

question: How is Mahdi's (1988) chain of changes, read in Adelaar (1991: 9), entered?
chosen_reading: Composed onto the nodes in the database: his PAN > Proto-Barito > Proto-East Barito > PSEB columns as rows of PSEB against Proto-Barito (which carries the PMP inventory, not Mahdi's Proto-Barito with *D and *z), then PMLG against PSEB and Merina against PMLG, all with source mahdi1988 via adelaar1991: 9. Only changes are entered; identities stay implied. His Proto-East Barito is not a node; his PAN (no *r, *z, *c, *T; *w and *y as vowels; preglottalised *b, *C, *j) is restated in PMP terms.
alternatives: Enter Mahdi's Proto-Barito and Proto-East Barito as nodes of their own; enter every line of the table including identities.

question: How are Adelaar's (1994a) Tamanic data and classification entered?
chosen_reading: As an earlier stage Pre-Tamanic (Glottolog's Tamanic, tama1334) under PMP, carrying Table 1's Tamanic column and the examples of §3.1, with Embaloh, Kalis (Glottolog's dialect of Embaloh) and Taman under it. Its subgrouping with South Sulawesi goes in as alt_parents pss (a proposed grouping), since Adelaar's PMP > Tamanic changes cannot be restated through Mills's PSS (Tamanic keeps final consonants PSS merged). Adelaar's preferred Tamanic-Buginese node (Glottolog's Tamanic-Bugis, bugi1243) is not entered.
alternatives: Put Pre-Tamanic under PSS and restate its rows; or add a Tamanic-Bugis group under PSS with Bugis and Pre-Tamanic.

question: Did Proto-Malayic keep the schwa in final closed syllables, and where does Jakarta Malay go?
chosen_reading: Both readings are entered on Proto-Malayic: Smith's (2017a) PMP *e > *a / _C# and Adelaar's (1992) retention of *ə (read via Adelaar 1995: 340); Jakarta Malay (Betawi, beta1252) goes directly under Proto-Malayic with its schwa as a stated retention (Adelaar 1994b). No Southwest Malay or Bangka grouping is entered.
alternatives: Follow Smith only and mark the Jakarta Malay e as a loan stratum (Grijns 1991); add Nothofer's Southwest Malay group.

question: How are Adelaar's (1992) Proto-Malayic innovations entered?
chosen_reading: As rows of Proto-Malayic (Smith's node, mala1538) against PMP, source adelaar1992 read via Adelaar (2004: 12), with the details of Adelaar (1994a: 5, Table 1) in the notes. PAn is restated against PMP: *-ey and *-ew are the schwa + glide (PMP keys e + y, e + w); *h and *ʔ are PMP *h. *q > *h is entered word-finally only, as Smith (2017a) has it, since Smith's Malayic lects are stated against a PM *q elsewhere; for the same reason innovations 3 (*z > PM *j) and 4 (*R > PM *r) are not entered as rows: Smith (2017a) states his Malayic lects from PMP *z and *R directly, and their rows rest on a PM *z and *R. Innovations 5 (reduction of clusters to their last component) and 6 (homorganic nasals in heterorganic NC) concern clusters and are in the notes only.
alternatives: Wait for Adelaar (1992) itself; enter the 1994a PML column as a separate set of rows.

question: How are Adelaar's (2012) Proto-South East Barito and Proto-Malagasy placed, and his PAN etyma entered?
chosen_reading: PSEB (Glottolog's Southeast Barito, sout2919) under Proto-Barito, with PMLG (Malagasic, mala1537) under it. PAN is restated against PMP, which Proto-Barito inherits (PAN *S and *h = PMP *h; *C, *T = *t; *ł = *n). Ma'anyan and Dusun Witu stay under Proto-Barito with Smith's (2017a) rows; moving them under PSEB would leave Smith's Proto-Barito rows on the wrong parent. Mahdi's (1988) Proto-East Barito (Adelaar 1991: 9) is not entered as a node. Rows marked 'from the examples' follow the cited etyma, not a stated rule.
alternatives: Move Ma'anyan (and Samihim, Dusun Witu) under PSEB, restating Smith's rows; or list Ma'anyan as a proposed daughter of PSEB through alt_parents; enter Proto-East Barito.

question: Which Malagasy varieties are entered, and with which Glottocodes?
chosen_reading: Merina (meri1243, a dialect of Glottolog's Plateau Malagasy, plt, entered as its language node), Sakalava (saka1291; Adelaar's 2012 SSK and 2013 Sakalava of Morondava), North Sakalava (no Glottolog languoid, code blank), Bara, Tandroy, Tankarana, Tsimihety, South Betsimisaraka (Ruud's, sout2920), Tanosy, and Old South East Malagasy (the Sorabe texts of Ferrand 1904, Adelaar's 2012 'Old Taimoro') as an attested language with no Glottocode. All directly under PMLG. Flacourt's (1658) data (2012 'Old SBM', 2013 a Tanosy source) are cited in notes, not entered as a lect. Antaisaka, Betsileo, Tanala, Vezo, Masikoro and Mahafaly, cited for single forms, are not entered.
alternatives: A separate Old South Betsimisaraka (Flacourt) lect; Betsileo, Antaisaka and Tanala as dialects of Plateau Malagasy and Tesaka; Glottolog's Malagasic subgroups as groups.

question: Which IPA for the Malagasy affricates tr and ts and the paragogic vowels?
chosen_reading: tr = ʈ͡ʂ (a retroflex affricate, Adelaar 2012: §4), ts = t͡s; Ruud's SBM final r and the Sorabe geminated r as ʈ͡ʂ, as Adelaar reads them; the paragogic (whispered) vowel after -tr, -ts, -k, -n is not part of the reflex and is given in the notes; o = u (Adelaar's own respelling); final y = i.
alternatives: ʈʳ or ʈ͡ɽ for tr; t͡ʃ for the southwestern ts; the paragogic vowel as part of the reflex (ʈ͡ʂə̆).

question: Is a subgrouping of the Malagasy dialects entered?
chosen_reading: No: all lects sit directly under Proto-Malagasy. Adelaar (2013) rejects Dez's (1963) li/ti division on methodological and distributional grounds (li and ti are retentions), finds the lexicostatistical classifications (Vérin, Kottak & Gorlin 1969; Mahdi 1988; Simon 2006) weak, and only tentatively groups the northern dialects with the central and eastern ones (Northern-Central-Eastern) against the southwestern ones, leaving the western dialects (Sakalava, West Bara) open (pp. 476-477). The *li > di, *ti > tsi and final *i/*e rows mark the evidence on the lects.
alternatives: Enter a Northern-Central-Eastern group and a Southwestern group; or Glottolog's Malagasic subgroups (North-Central, Southwestern).

question: How are Goodenough's (1992) PMc > Chuukese vowel changes entered?
chosen_reading: As rows of Chuukese against Proto-Chuukic (Goodenough's PTk, which keeps the PMc vowels and the central [ɨ] of *u as ɨ, as Jackson's 1984 rows have it), derivation composed. Sequences of unlike vowels that became double vowels (§2.3.1) are entered as cluster rows on both members (V1 > VV / _+V2, V2 > VV / V1+_); 'in some cases' is sporadic; changes stated as one of two outcomes have conditioning unknown. Vowel length is IPA ː; Goodenough's ú é á ó are ɨ ə æ ɔ as in Goodenough & Sugita (1980). The Kiribati and Woleaian statements, made against POc, are entered against their parents (PCMC, PCK).
alternatives: Enter only the single-vowel changes (§§2.3.2-2.3.6) and leave §2.3.1 and the final-vowel loss to the notes.

question: How is Bugenhagen's (1994) Mangap-Mbula entered beside Ross's (1988) consonant rows?
chosen_reading: Table 1 as Mangap's sourced inventory (prenasalised stops ᵐb ⁿd ᵑɡ beside oral b d ɡ, y = j); Table 3 and the voiced-stop statement (p. 51) as rows against POC by position (fortis/lenis initial, intervocalic, developed final), and the vowel rules 1-6 (pp. 53-59) as conditioned rows; Ross's rows are kept. Ross writes the prenasalised stops b, d, g (his orthography); Bugenhagen's mb, nd, ŋg are the same sounds.
alternatives: Enter only the inventory and leave the reflexes to Ross (1988).

question: Harrison (1994: 329-333) repeats Jackson's (1983) POC > PMC > GIL consonant charts. What is entered?
chosen_reading: Only what the rows of Bender et al. (2003a) and the other sources do not already state: the *u and *e splits, *w > Ø before round vowels (as disputed, since Harrison doubts such *w), the t/k assimilation and dissimilation (sporadic, few cases), high-vowel loss after nasals, sporadic *a loss, and the dialect allophones of /t/ before u. All restated against PCMc.
alternatives: Enter the full charts as further rows against PCMc.

question: How are Holzknecht's (1994) Markham and Lower-Markham innovations entered?
chosen_reading: Composed onto Labu only, through PHG, PMK and PLMK (not nodes here, as for Ross 1988), with the vowel splits as irregular rows and the Bukawa loans with t as a loan stratum. The other Markham languages, already entered from Ross (1988), get no rows from this chapter, which cites them as examples, not as correspondence tables. Holzknecht's subgroups (Upper Markham, Watut, Lower Markham) are not added as groups.
alternatives: Add Markham and Lower Markham as groups (Glottolog mark1257, lowe1411) under POC; or compose the innovations onto every Markham language.

question: How are Ozanne-Rivierre's (1994) Fagauvea data entered?
chosen_reading: Pawley's (1967) PNP > WUV table as rows of pawley1967 via this chapter; the voicing of t and k in grammatical morphemes and the irregular h in Polynesian loans as rows of this chapter (the latter a loan stratum); the *m, *n splits as disputed, since the author rejects them; Hollyman's (1987: 21) system as the sourced inventory via this chapter (tr dr = ʈ ɖ, j = ɟ, hw = ʍ, th = θ, sh = ʃ, hl = ɬ, ü = y), with hm, hn and the flap as marginal.
alternatives: Enter the splits as regular rows, as Pawley and Hollyman have them.

question: Where do Reid's (1994) Alta and Arta go, and against what are their reflexes stated?
chosen_reading: Northern Alta, Southern Alta (under a group Altan) and Arta under Proto-Northern Luzon, as in Reid's (2006) tree, whose primary branches include Altan and Arta; their reflexes, which Reid gives against Proto-Philippines and Proto-Cordilleran, are entered against PNL (Proto-Cordilleran). Loans that Reid identifies by g < *R, g < *j or k are a loan stratum. The lects inherit what Reid does not discuss (assumed-unchanged).
alternatives: Put the Alta languages under a Meso-Cordilleran node (Glottolog meso1254), as Reid's (1994: 452) genetic argument suggests.

question: How are Rivierre's (1994) PNC reflexes and the Kone chart entered?
chosen_reading: Table 4 as rows against PNC on Pwapwâ, Pwaamei and Haveke (Kone), initial position. Rivierre's *t̲, *ṭ, *c (and doubles) are the sheet's PNC *t, *ṭ, *s (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992's spelling): his dentals become palatals (*t̲- > c), his palatals retroflexes (*c- > t) and his retroflexes stay (*ṭ- > t). The KON column goes on Haveke with Haveke's θ, ð for KON s, y (chart, p. 519). The Haveke chart, loans included, is Haveke's sourced inventory. Pwaamei y = ʝ (a voiced palatal spirant, p. 517). Caac is added under PNC with Hollyman's (1962) consonants via Rivierre.
alternatives: Enter the KON column on a separate Kone lect, or as printed (s, y) on Haveke.

question: How are Ross's (1994) New Ireland reconstructions entered?
chosen_reading: As three proto-language nodes, the user's choice of 26 November 2026: Proto-New Ireland under POC (Glottocode blank, its inventory (1) only; no POC > PNI rows, which the chapter does not give), Proto-Lavongai/Nalik (tung1294) and Proto-Madak (mada1284) under PNI, with Nalik, Kara, Tiang, Tigak and Lavongai under PLN, Barok, Madak and Lamasong under PMAD, and Patpatar directly under PNI, as in tables (2) and (3). Symbols: y = j, Nalik and Kara f = ɸ, Madak v = β, γ = ɣ. Rule (11) and rule (30) are allophones. Kuot (Papuan) and Notsi (Tabar) are not entered.
alternatives: Hold the nodes back and compose the daughters onto POC through Ross (1988), as the user chose for Ross (1988) on 24 November 2026.

question: How is Tryon's (1994) Appendix 1 (POC consonants in 17 Eastern Outer Islands lects) entered?
chosen_reading: Grace's POC symbols read as Ross's (mp = b, nt = d, ŋk = ɡ, ŋp = bʷ, ŋm = mʷ, d and r = r, nd = dr, ns = j). Each reflex is restated against the lect's parent: the Temotu lects through the sheet's chain (POC > PTm > PRSC, PUtupua, PVanikoro), the Outliers against PNP through POC > PPN > PNP (p > f, b and bʷ > p, d > t, ɡ > k, q > ʔ, r and dr > l, mʷ > ŋ, ñ > n; *j, *y, *R lost), since the sheet's POC > PCP rows are incomplete. Cells whose phoneme the parent does not have are not entered: lost in the parent, or, for PRSC *p- and *ñ, not stated in the sheet (Lackey & Boerger 2021 give PRSC *p only between vowels) (18 cells: Reefs *p- '∅, v1, p2'; Reefs *-p- '∅'; Malo *p- '∅, v4, p5, pʷ6'; Malo *-p- 'p, ∅7'; Lwepe *p- '∅, v4, p5, pʷ6'; Lwepe *-p- 'p, ∅7, w7'; Nanggu *p- 'p, v9'; Nanggu *-p- 'p, ᵐbʷ7'; Ontong Java *ns- '∅, s8'; Sikaiana *ns- '∅, s8'; Tikopia *ns- '∅, s8'; Reefs *ñ- 'n'; Malo *ñ- '∅2 (?)'; Lwepe *ñ- '∅2 (?)'; Nanggu *ñ- '∅2 (?)'; Nembao *-R- 'j'; Asumboa *-R- 'l'; Tanimbili *-R- 'j'). The first reflex in a cell is regular; footnoted ones are conditioned where the footnote gives a condition ('Mainly before non-low back vowels'), regular with conditions unknown where it says 'unconditioned', a loan stratum where it says 'borrowing', disputed where it says 'uncertain' or '(?)', sporadic otherwise. Malo and Lwepe are new Santa Cruz dialects of Natügu (Lwepe sharing Natügu's code), Pileni (Vaeakau-Taumako) a new Outlier under PNP. Printed y = j, ñ = ɲ, mb nd ŋg = ᵐb ⁿd ᵑɡ (b d ɡ in Buma, as in Teanu's sourced inventory), nj̆ = ᶮɟ, ǰ = d͡ʒ; Asumboa mu for *ŋm and Malo, Lwepe u for *w- are read as mʷ and w.
alternatives: Enter the rows against POC as printed, as in Tryon, without restating; or leave the Outliers out.

question: The North and Central Vanuatu lects stood in three places under Southern Oceanic: under PNCV, loose under the linkage (five Malakula languages), and in a group Central Vanuatu beside PNCV (South Efate, Naman, Nese). How are they arranged?
chosen_reading: One clade North and Central Vanuatu (Proto-North-Central Vanuatu, nort3195) with two groups, Northern Vanuatu (nort3205) and Central Vanuatu (cent2269), as in Glottolog 5.4 and Clark (2009). Every lect is listed under its group. The lects whose rows Lynch states against POc keep parent_id poc (they inherit from POc and their rows are POc > lect) and have tree_parent central-vanuatu: since 26 November 2026 a tree parent may stand below the lect's parent_id. PNCV stays their proposed parent (alt_parents pncv:clark2009), now also for V'ënen Taut, Tirax, Malua-Tepërav, Botovro and Vao.
alternatives: Leave the POc-stated lects outside PNCV (as on 24 November); restate them against PNCV once PNCV has consonants; no Northern Vanuatu group.
notes: The user's item 'North and Central Vanuatu problem' of 26 November 2026, read as the scattering of the lects; revert if something else was meant.

question: The user asked (26 November 2026) for Gayo, Mentawai and Enggano to be split into dialects with their own pages under Pre-Gayo, Pre-Mentawai and Pre-Enggano. Which dialects, and what is stated of each?
chosen_reading: Gayo: five dialects under Pre-Gayo (Bukit, Cik, Dëret, Lues, Serbejadi; Billings & McDonnell 2024: 117), each stated-unchanged apart from the two sets: *ay, *aw > aɪ, aʊ in Lues and e, o in Bukit and Dëret, not attested for Cik and Serbejadi; the funny nasals with their generational merger on Bukit only (Eades 2005 is a grammar of Bukit), not attested for the other four. Glottolog's Dorot = Dëret and Serbodjadi = Serbejadi; Bukit, Cik and Lues have no Glottocode. Enggano: Southern and Western Enggano under Pre-Enggano with the columns of Table 10. The language-level lects gayo1244 and engg1245 are retired and Pre-Gayo and Pre-Enggano carry their Glottocodes (as Pre-Nasal and Pre-Basap do). Mentawai: only Simalegi (sima1259) is split off, with *s, *t > t; the lect Mentawai keeps the three sets whose varieties the source does not name.
alternatives: Keep language nodes Gayo and Enggano over the dialects; put the funny-nasal rows on all five Gayo dialects; split Mentawai into Glottolog's nine dialects once Pampus (1989, 1994) and Blust (1997) are read.
notes: Billings & McDonnell (2024) read again from the PDF on 26 November 2026. No sourced inventories were added: the dialects' inventories are generated from Pre-X and the rows. Eades & Hajek (2006, JIPA 36: 107-115) has a Bukit inventory; not read.

question: Ross (1988) prints the Papuan Tip consonant correspondences (Tables 28-30) as POC > PPT > language, and for the Central Papuan family as POC > PPT > PCP > language. Against which stage are the rows stated?
chosen_reading: Against Proto-Papuan Tip (ppt), an established node already in the tree, with PPT in the sheet's Oceanic spelling (*bw bʷ, *mw mʷ, *pw pʷ, *kw kʷ, *gw ɡʷ, *g ɡ); the rows are direct, not composed. POC > PPT: the mergers and the split of *p into *p and *v (p. 196) are added; the split of *k and the merger of *ñ were already entered from Lynch et al. (2002). PPT *gw has no POC source and is a manual-add phoneme; PPT *pw and *kw, for which Ross (1988) prints no POC source either, continue the sheet's POc *pʷ and *kʷ. PPT *s fortis and lenis are one phoneme, the grade named in the environment when the two cells differ. Proto Central Papuan (Table 30) is held back like Ross's other intermediate reconstructions (decision ross1988-composition): the Central Papuan rows are composed PPT > language with the PCP value in as_printed, and the column POC *Ø- (PCP *y before *a) is not entered. A bracketed reflex is a loan-stratum row. Hyphens, ';', ',' and the superscripts as in ross1988-composition. Not entered: Wedau and Taupota *y, printed as a small capital D (p. 200); Table 31 (a postposition, not a correspondence).
alternatives: Compose every row POC > language as in the North New Guinea batch; or add Proto Central Papuan as a node.

question: How are Ross's (1988) Papuan Tip language names matched to Glottolog and to lects?
chosen_reading: By Ross's own equations (Figures 7-8: Paiwa = Gapapaiwa, Kukuya = Minaveha, Gumasi = Gumawana, Kakabai = Igora; Lala = Nara, p. 190) and Glottolog 5.4 and Ross et al. (2023): Boianaki = Ghayavi, Garuwahi = Gweda, Kalokalo = Koluwawa, Yamalele = Iamalele, Bosilewa = Boselewa, Kurada = 'Auhelawa, Tubetube = Bwanabwana, Bohutu = Buhutu, Gabadi = Abadi, Doura = Toura (tour1243), Bina = bina1271. Dialects under their language: Arifama and Miniafia (Arifama-Miniafia), Kwato and Daui (Suau), Iwa and Gawa (Muyuw, whose own row is the language's), Madawa, Pamela and Varavarae (Sudest), West Mekeo (Mekeo), Balawaia and Taboro (Sinaugoro), Aroma (Keapara); Hula is a language, as in Glottolog. Dialects with no Glottolog code share the language's (Kwato, Gawa, Madawa, Varavarae). Fagululu is not identified (no glottocode). All are under ppt; Ross's networks and chains (Figures 6-9) are in the notes, not nodes.
alternatives: Other matches; network and chain nodes below PPT.

question: Ross (1988) prints the North-West Solomonic consonant correspondences (Table 32) as POC > PNS > (PNN, PCH, PNGe, PYS) > language. Against which stage are the rows stated?
chosen_reading: Against POc, composed, as in the North New Guinea batch (ross1988-composition): Proto North-West Solomonic and the four lower reconstructions are not nodes in the tree, so they are held back and their values kept in as_printed; every language is under POc with tree_parent mm. Fortis and lenis grades are named in the environment. POC *s, *c: where Ross prints one value (Solos to Mono-Alu) no grade is named. The column POC *-q is POC-final *q. Two cells are changed for the parser (see ross1988_t32.py): Taiof *r, *R 'ŋ/_#i' is read '_*i#'.
alternatives: A Proto-North-West Solomonic node (PNS) with the languages stated against it, as for Proto-Papuan Tip; or nodes for PNN, PCH, PNGe and PYS as well.

question: How are Ross's (1988) North-West Solomonic language names matched to Glottolog and to lects?
chosen_reading: By Glottolog 5.4 names and alternate names: Piva = Lawunuia, Sengga = Sisiqa (the existing lect), Nduke = Duke, Kia = Zabana, Ghove = Gao, Maringe = Cheke Holo (the language; Glottolog's Maringe is one of its dialects). Selau is a dialect of Halia in Glottolog and is a dialect lect under Halia here; Taiof keeps its existing language lect (a dialect of Saposa in Glottolog). The five lects with a sourced inventory (Taiof, Banoni, Sisiqa, Roviana, Kokota) take Ross's letters in that inventory's symbols (Taiof c = t͡s, Banoni t = t̪, Kokota v = v); elsewhere Ross's v is β and c is t͡ʃ.
alternatives: Maringe as the Maringe dialect of Cheke Holo; Selau as a language.

question: Ross (1988) Table 34 prints the Meso-Melanesian consonant correspondences as POC > (PWZ, PLN, PTAB, PMAD) > language; Proto-Lavongai/Nalik (pln) and Proto-Madak (pmad) are nodes already (Ross 1994). Against which stage are the rows stated?
chosen_reading: The user's choice of 26 November 2026: the Lavongai/Nalik languages against pln and the Madak languages against pmad, the rest composed from POc. A row is stated against the node when Ross's PLN or PMAD value for the column is one phoneme of the node's inventory (PLN *p, *f, *b, *u = *w, *m, *t, *d, *n, *l, *r = *R, *s, *y, *k, *g, *ŋ; PMAD *p, *b, *u = *w, *m, *t, *n, *s, i = *y, *k, *g, *ŋ). The other columns of those languages (POC *mw, *j, lenis *k and *q, the initial set of PLN *Y; for Madak also lenis *p, *d, *l, *r) are composed from POC with parent_lect_id poc, because the node has no single phoneme for them or Ross's value is conditioned. Patpatar (under pni) is composed from POC in the same way. Bali-Vitu, the Willaumez and Tabar chains, the South New Ireland languages and Tomoip are under POc (tree_parent mm), PWZ and PTAB held back with their values in as_printed. The POC > PWZ, PLN, PTAB, PMAD and PNS rows of the table are not entered.
alternatives: Everything composed from POc.

question: How are Ross's (1988) Meso-Melanesian language names matched to Glottolog and to lects?
chosen_reading: By Glottolog 5.4: Bali = Uneapa (the existing lect), Vitu = Muduapa, Tabar = Mandara, Tolai = Kuanua, Duke of York = Ramoaaina, Lavongai = Tungag, Lamasong = the existing Lamasong dialect lect; Bola (Harua) is Glottolog's Harua dialect of Bola; Kara (E) and Kara (W) are East Kara and West Kara, dialect lects under the existing Kara. Lects that have rows or an inventory already keep their symbols for Ross's v and f (Lavongai v, Nalik and Kara ɸ, Siar ɸ); elsewhere v is β. The new South New Ireland and Tabar lects are under POc with tree_parent mm, like Siar and Tomoip, not under pni.
alternatives: The South New Ireland and Tabar languages under Proto-New Ireland (pni), like Patpatar.

question: Ross (1988) Table 36 prints the Admiralties consonant correspondences as POC > PAd > (PWAd, PEAd) > language, with secondary oral and nasal grades, and Table 37 the PAd secondary nasal grade phonemes. Against which stage are the rows stated?
chosen_reading: Against Proto-Admiralty (padm), an established node whose phonemes are those of POc (inherit), with PWAd and PEAd held back and their values in as_printed; Mussau and Tench (St Matthias, outside the Admiralties) are composed from POc. POC *R is composed from POc with parent_lect_id poc, because padm has no *R (Lynch et al. 2002: *R > *y before high vowels, lost elsewhere), while Ross's PAd keeps medial *-R-; for the eastern languages its three columns are 'before *a', 'before *o', 'before *i, *u'. Secondary nasal grade (the reflex after the POC article *na, pp. 339-340): Table 37's putative PAd *mp-, *nt-, *ns-, *ŋk- are added to padm by hand (ᵐp, ⁿt, ⁿs, ᵑk) and the secondary nasal columns of Table 36 are stated against them, that of *r against PAd *dr, with which it merged; the environment says 'secondary nasal grade'. PAd *-f- (medial *p) is not a padm phoneme: the *p cells are stated against *p. Fortis and lenis *s are named in the environment. Ross's dr is ⁿr, nh is left as printed. Not entered: the PAd, PWAd and PEAd rows themselves; the first reflex of Sori-Harengan *q (unread glyph).
alternatives: Everything composed from POc, as for North-West Solomonic; or PWAd and PEAd as nodes.

question: How are Ross's (1988) St Matthias and Admiralties language names matched to Glottolog and to lects?
chosen_reading: By Glottolog 5.4: Tench = Tenis, Lindrou = Nyindrou, Mokoreng = Mokerang, Koro = Manus Koro (bowa1234), Kaniet = kani1282 (not Kaniet-Dempwolff). Varieties that Glottolog makes dialects are dialect lects under a language node: Aua and Wuvulu (Wuvulu-Aua), Baluan (Baluan-Pam), Pak (Pak-Tong), Bohuai (Tulu-Bohuai), Andra and Hus (Andra-Hus, sharing andr1248). Levei-Tulu has no glottocode: Glottolog puts Levei under Khehek (leve1237) and Tulu under Tulu-Bohuai (tulu1260), and Ross's one column covers both (they differ in two cells, his dagger). Tenis is under POc beside Mussau; the Admiralties lects are under padm.
alternatives: Levei-Tulu as Khehek (kheh1237); Andra and Hus as one lect.

question: Shibata (2020) Tables 4.2-4.13 give the reflexes of every Proto-Bunun phoneme in the five dialects, and Tables 6.11 and 6.13 the same through Proto-Northern and Proto-Central Bunun. The dialects had only the rows of the changes (decision li-bunun-dialects, reverted: no inherit). Enter the retentions?
chosen_reading: Yes, as rows with the examples of Tables 4.3-4.12: Takituduh and Takibakha against Proto-Northern Bunun (Table 6.11), Takbanuað and Takivatan against Proto-Central Bunun (Table 6.13; no *c row, it merged with *s there), Isbukun against Proto-Bunun. The vowels (Table 4.12) are stated by Shibata against Proto-Bunun and entered against each dialect's parent. Not entered again: *b and *d (rows of Li 1988, Jiang 2012 and Shibata 2020: 38, 46 are in for every dialect), and Isbukun *q, *ʔ, *c, *h, *l (in from Tables 4.2-4.10). Not entered: the six diphthongs of Table 4.13 (not phonemes of the Proto-Bunun inventory here; Takibakha e, o are in from Jiang 2012).
alternatives: Give the dialects inherit (stated-unchanged) with Shibata's tables as the source instead of rows; or state all rows against Proto-Bunun with parent_lect_id.

question: Song (2025) chapter 7 (Tables 7.1-7.8) gives the evidence for Toda-Truku, Toda and Truku as changes of Proto-Toda-Truku, Proto-Toda and Proto-Truku. How are they entered, the subgroups being groups without proto-languages (decision song-seediq)?
chosen_reading: On each dialect, against Song's Proto-Seediq (system Song), beside the rows of Tables 4.3-4.23. New rows: *ə > i before y, > u before w, and full assimilation to a following vowel (Tables 7.1-7.2, with 4.22-4.23) for Central Toda and the two Truku dialects; initial *gə- > u- for Central and Eastern Toda (Table 7.5), and *ə > u next to *g elsewhere as sporadic; the sporadic changes of Table 7.3 (Central Toda, Central and Eastern Truku) and of Table 7.8 (Truku), each with its etymon in lexical_scope. Eastern Toda gets only the rows for which Song prints an Eastern Toda form (he has little data, pp. 155-156). Not entered: Table 7.5's *g > w, Table 7.6's *c > s and Table 7.7's *t, *d > c, ɟ before *i (already in from Tables 4.4, 4.8, 4.9, 4.13); the loss of *rə- in *rəsənaw > sənaw; Truku *aw > u after a coronal (*sawni > suni), because the diphthongs are not entered (song-seediq); Central Truku gisak from *gəsak; the lexical innovations of Tables 7.4, 7.9, 7.10.
alternatives: Make Toda-Truku, Toda and Truku proto-languages (Song writes PTo-TR and PTR forms) and state these changes once on each.

question: Lobel (2013) chapter 9 (Tables 9.1-9.7): Proto-Danaw and Maranao. Which node, which predecessor, and how are the heavy consonants written and derived?
chosen_reading: New node Proto-Danaw (pdan, dana1253) under Proto-Greater Central Philippine with Allison's (1979) inventory as Lobel prints it (Table 9.1), and Maranao (mara1404) under it. Table 9.2's third column is headed 'PSPH/PGCPH'; its rows are stated against pgcph, the node already in the data. Rows on pdan: *h > ∅ and ʔ, *b > *w, *d and *l > *r (conditions not given), *a > *ə in prepenultimate syllables. Maranao: the heavy consonants are written pʼ tʼ kʼ sʼ (Lobel's p’ t’ k’ s’, with the modifier apostrophe; they are aspirated, not ejective) and derived by two rows per cluster (*p > pʼ after *b, *b > ∅ before *p, and so on), since Proto-Danaw *bp, *dt, *ds, *gk are clusters, not phonemes; *u > o; y and r respelled j and ɾ; /h/ marginal; the two vowel sets of Tables 9.5-9.6 and the implosives as allophones. Iranun and Maguindanaon are not entered (no table gives their reflexes).
alternatives: Write the heavy consonants pʰ tʰ kʰ sʰ; enter *bp, *dt, *ds, *gk as Proto-Danaw phonemes; hold Proto-Danaw back and state Maranao against PGCPH.
notes: The standing rule for Lobel enters established microgroups and holds back the nodes above them; Danao is the microgroup.

question: Lobel (2013) Tables 11.13a-c and 11.23 give forms and innovations for 35 Dusunic, Bisaya-Lotud and Murutic languages that were not lects. Which lects, which Glottocodes, and which rows?
chosen_reading: 35 new lects under Proto-Dusunic (16), Proto-Bisaya-Lotud (4) and Proto-Murutic (15), with the level and code of the matching Glottolog languoid, and three language nodes where Glottolog puts several of Lobel's varieties in one language: Kadazan Dusun (Tindal = Tempasuk Dusun, Tinagas = Kota Marudu Tinagas, Tambunan, Penampang = Coastal Kadazan; representative Tambunan), Brunei Bisaya-Dusun (Brunei Dusun, Limbang Bisaya = Brunei Bisaya) and Abai (Sembuak, Tubu; one code). No code: Dusun Membakut, Dusun Kimanis, Dusun Papar, Tingalan. Talantang is kota1279, Tidung the Glottolog family node tidu1239 (ISO tid). Rows: only what the tables are about, the reflexes of *R, stated through the proto-language above each language: PDUS and PBISLO *h kept or lost (Table 11.13b and the last column of Table 11.23, read as the key's item 16), final *w and *g kept (Tables 11.13a, c), PMUR final *g > g, ɣ, h, ŋ, k (Table 11.13a); for the Dusunic languages also *ə > o, kept in Kujau and Minokok, from the text of p. 385 (the Minokok forms all have o). Also new: Limbang Bisaya *iw > uy; PGDUS *a > *ə (Table 11.18); PGMUR final-syllable *ə > *o; the loss of root-initial *g after *ma- in Proto-Murutic and Papar (Table 11.21); final *g and *h kept in Papar, final *g in Tatana. The other reflexes the forms show (r > z, l, y; l > h; w > v; y > z, j; the printed £) are not entered, so these lects' inventories are mostly inherited and incomplete.
alternatives: Enter no lects from lexeme tables; or read every phoneme off the forms; or put the Glottolog dialects directly under Proto-Dusunic without language nodes.
